title: Beige Book — July 16, 2025
html:
Official report: Summary · Full PDF Local PDF: 2025-07-16 Beige Book.pdf

Overall economic activity

Activity rose slightly. Five Districts reported slight or modest gains, five were flat and two reported modest declines—an improvement from the prior report, when half the Districts saw declines. Uncertainty stayed elevated and kept businesses cautious. Manufacturing edged lower, construction slowed (rising costs constrained some projects), energy declined slightly and agriculture remained weak. Home sales were flat in most Districts and nonresidential real estate mostly steady. Loan volume rose slightly in most Districts. The outlook was neutral to slightly pessimistic; only two Districts expected activity to increase. The report was prepared by the Boston Fed.

Consumer spending

Non-auto spending fell in most Districts. Auto sales dipped modestly after earlier buying to beat tariffs. Tourism was mixed.

Labor markets

Employment rose very slightly: one District reported modest gains, six slight gains, three no change and two slight declines. Hiring stayed cautious, often tied to policy uncertainty. Labor availability improved, with lower turnover and more applicants, but more Districts reported skilled-trades shortages. Several Districts reported fewer foreign-born workers due to immigration policy changes. Wages rose modestly. Layoffs were limited, though somewhat more common among manufacturers.

Prices

Prices rose in all Districts—seven moderate, five modest. All twelve Districts reported tariff-related input cost pressure, especially for manufacturing and construction materials. Rising insurance costs were widespread. Input costs outpaced selling prices; some firms passed costs along, while others held back because of price-sensitive customers, squeezing margins. Contacts expected cost pressures to persist, with consumer prices possibly starting "to rise more rapidly by late summer."

Notable themes

  • Tariffs: Universal input-cost pressure.
  • AI/automation: A few employers boosted investment to reduce future hiring needs.
  • Immigration: Reduced availability of foreign-born workers.
  • Uncertainty: Many firms deferring major hiring and layoff decisions.

District highlights

  • Boston: Tourism edged down, partly from fewer Canadian visitors.
  • New York, Philadelphia: Modest declines.
  • Cleveland: Transportation demand dropped sharply; costs rose robustly.
  • Richmond: Moderate growth.
  • Kansas City: Labor availability much higher, lowering expected wage pressure.
  • Dallas: Slight growth, but outlook pessimistic.
  • St. Louis: Outlook highly uncertain and slightly pessimistic.

Read-through for SPY

  • A return to slight growth eased fears of a downturn after the June report.
  • Squeezed margins and expected faster consumer inflation by late summer were risks for earnings and rate-cut hopes.
  • Early AI-driven hiring substitution is a productivity theme worth tracking.
